comments.text:
You ask whether these toxic cities, with their massive slums and people living literally in rubbish dumps—making a living by recycling and eating—are a sign of bad governance. Let me first say this: look at these countries a couple of hundred years ago. There was no pollution like this until the white man showed up. When the white man leaves, that’s when you get the slums, the filth dumps, the poor people. The most recent iteration of this is Papua New Guinea. People were basically living naked in tree houses and cannibalizing each other, or so the story goes; they’re no longer doing that now. Now they’ve got slums, guns, gangs, while some businesses owned by foreign entities are exploiting their gold. This is what you get when these people touch your country. The other thing is that some clowns thought it was a good idea to create a consumer-based economy driven by consumerism. If consumerism stalls, the entire economy stalls. So, they tell us—so they, the governments, have designed a system where the people think they’re just being taxed. Taxed in all sorts of different little ways, and apparently, you’re just not supposed to pay too much attention to it. Then you have the banks colluding with these governments to eat away at everybody’s funds for every little thing they can nail you for. Bang, bang, bang, bang. They take a huge portion of money they didn’t work for, leaving people with no money. That is the point. You’re allowed to have the little bit of money you get from that nonsense they call work. At the same time, there are constraints on human capacity, constraints on resources, constraints on water. These economists love to tell everybody, “No, no, you can’t have money—it’s inflationary, you see, and there are constraints on resources.” Then they’ll look at somebody else and say, “You know, the economy is doing so great. GDP is outpacing the debt.” Suddenly those constraints don’t matter. We’ve got absurd people who think they’ve been educated with objective science, and never do they question who decided which basket constitutes inflation, or what gets included in the equations. Well, actually, inflationary assets are excluded—and this is where biased assumptions and mathematics that the bankers know how to weaponize, and have weaponized for a long time, get taught to people. 

Economists absorb this and think they’re just absorbing innocent knowledge from innocent people who want to raise society. What they’re doing is something they don’t even understand. When they scream about inflation, it’s a generalization. When they talk about asset appreciation, it’s a generalization. It’s not asset inflation; it’s asset appreciation, you see. Then they convince the people, like Pavlovian dogs: when you ring the little bell, they salivate and get very angry and say, “No, you can’t have money, it’s inflationary.” But can I convince you at the same time to buy an inflationary asset? What might just remind this short-sighted person, who doesn’t seem to have any memory, that you just said I can’t have purchasing power because it’s inflationary. Now you’re telling me I must go buy an inflationary asset? These are the kind of people we’re dealing with on this planet. So anyway, the reason the government makes sure people have no money is to try to force consumerism onto them—consume, consume, consume. That’s why, when you fork out ten years’ salary on a computer or a laptop, it lasts two years and then you’ve got to replace it, because apparently people just have disposable income lying all over the place. The governments are printing so much money, and the stuff is just lying all over the place—you can just pick it up on the streets and go buy whatever the hell you want. Apparently, that’s the way. People make a noise about it, but in reality? No. Anyway, mobile phones and smartphones are the same. They are deliberately designed to last a couple of years while you pay the earth for them, I might add. People are not shy about charging prices that amount to a deposit for a car, for a phone, or a deposit for a house, or even a PlayStation. They’re pushing it with their nonsense. When the PlayStation 4 came out, 6,000 rand for that thing. And then when the PlayStation 5 came out, it was double—oh, more than double. And then everything’s locked behind a paywall, a subscription wall. Besides that, it’s just an example of how insane these people are.

So the trash is a result of the consumer-based economy and convenience—convenience for the people, inconvenience for the ecosystem, and eventually they end up inconveniencing themselves. But then, you know, these people innovate. One man’s trash is another man’s gold, apparently. But all this business that is supposedly legitimate and responsible—they say—a lot of them are just businesses for the sake of keeping jobs, really, and for the owner to profit a little bit. But they’re producing all of these materials and disposable products, one-use products: use once, discard; use another one, discard. Then you look at Western countries. You don’t see slums like this in the West, where people are living in filth as badly as they do in other countries, because they just hide their mountains of trash a little bit better. But it looks like a manicured mountain is hiding the trash—you know, nice grass, pipes sticking out of it. Anyway. I feel sorry for those people living in the trash, but unfortunately that is the way I see humanity. That is a reflection of humanity: trash. You can hear it in their voice, or you can hear it in their arguments. Work, dog-slave, or starve, dog-slave. Well, we sit here and tell you to do so while we pretend like we’re working and getting a salary for it, you know? Work produces more, pollute more. Quite frankly, I’ve passed the halfway mark of my life. My age? I’m not too bothered what happens with this planet and these people on this planet. The only thing that does bother me is: what if reincarnation is real and I have to come back and go through all this nonsense again? That’s not something I want. Besides, I was never consulted about coming to this place in the first place. My parents made that decision on my behalf, apparently. Then you arrive here and you must deal with everybody’s nonsense and fit into their indoctrinated way of thinking.

These modern-day places are sort of like medieval towns: open sewage running down the middle of the street, a pot in your room that you threw out the window straight into the road, animals, waste, food all mixed together. It is also a huge, toxic cocktail. But here’s what catches me the most: I don’t understand what it is with these people, how they still continue to start families in areas like that. Last night I watched Tucker Carlson’s show about the South African farm murders, and I was listening to this man talk about how his child was murdered, his wife. I was 11 years old when apartheid ended in South Africa. To answer your other question, that’s where I’m from. My first thought was: well, I’m not going to have children. Why? First of all, I’m not happy about the circumstances I find myself in, and the rules and regulations imposed on me. That’s not a world I want to bring my children into. And besides, these people who abolished apartheid don’t really truly understand what they’ve done—not that I’m defending apartheid, but they don’t really understand what they’ve done. Not that they came up today, anyway. Morality? That is Satanism. The new Satanism, apparently. And I also thought to myself: I will not bring a child into this world. Why? Because after apartheid was abolished, well, the father telling you what happened to his child is one of the reasons why I’ve chosen not to. I will not bring my child into a world like this, to come contribute to a nonsense society like this. Who believes the nonsense they do? Who takes the nonsense they do from the government and fights with each other while the government writes laws and hides behind bodyguards and their banks? Nobody’s looking at those people and thinking, okay, you know, instead of fighting with each other, maybe we should turn our attentions to these people and their policies. We don’t want to hear about inflation. We want to hear about hyperinflation. We have productive capacity. Those who want to make those noises must shut up. They’ve made enough and caused enough bloodshed. Walk into the middle of a crowd of people in the West specifically. Pull out your little bell. And ring it in the form of you saying we need purchasing power for the poor and watch everybody immediately get angry and say no, that's invasionary. Watch try it. These people are like Pavlovian dogs. You ring that little bell, they start salivating. Quick, too reflexively regurgitate. The unhealthy poison economists spew into their heads. Under the guise of education.

replies.text:
It wasn’t so long ago that first contact was made with Papua New Guineans. I think it was in the 1960s or 1970s. There’s a video on YouTube about that first contact. These people were still living like cave people, basically hunting together, just about naked. But as soon as somebody discovers gold, suddenly the pitch changes. We’re going to give you housing. We’re going to give you jobs. We’re going to give you banks. Except you’re going to be denied access to those houses. You’re going to be denied access to the banks. You’re going to be denied access to, well, everything we promised you. We just want your gold. Move, stupid, uneducated fool. Yes, thank you. I like that deal. Sounds like a great deal. Sounds like what the vast majority of people accept at face value and then pay for with their children. This is the same pattern everywhere. The promise is civilization, progress, opportunity. The reality is extraction. They dangle housing, jobs, banks, infrastructure, education—all the things that supposedly make you modern. But the fine print is always the same: you get access to just enough to keep you dependent, and never enough to be free. The gold, the oil, the minerals, the land—those get taken. The people get managed. The banks get to charge fees. The governments get to tax. The foreign companies get to profit. And the locals get to live in slums next to the wealth that was dug out of their own ground.

And what makes it worse is that people keep accepting the deal. Not because they’re stupid, but because the deal is presented as the only option. You’re told this is development. You’re told this is progress. You’re told this is what it means to be part of the modern world. So, you sign up. You take the job. You take the loan. You take the house you can’t really afford. You take the phone you can’t really pay for. You accept the taxes, the fees, the subscriptions, the updates, the inflation. And then you wonder why you never get ahead. The answer is simple: the game was never designed for you to get ahead. It was designed for you to keep playing. So, when I look at places like Papua New Guinea, or Nigeria, or South Africa, or any of these so-called developing countries, I don’t just see poverty. I see a system that promised everything and delivered just enough to keep people trapped. I see people who were told they were being brought into the modern world, only to find out that the modern world wanted their resources and their labor and their obedience, not their prosperity. And the saddest part is that most people still believe the promise. They still think if they just work harder, consume more, vote the right way, and obey the rules, things will get better. But the rules were written by the people who benefit from them. And until people see that, nothing changes. The deal stays the same. The gold leaves. The trash stays. And the children pay for it.

Let me add a caveat here, because I know some people will read what I said earlier—that when the white man touches a country, he leaves it looking like a slum—and they’ll immediately say, “Oh, so you hate white people. You support farm murders.” That is not what I’m saying. I do not support farm murders. I am not saying every white person is responsible for this. I am talking about a system. I use the phrase “white man” as shorthand for the colonial mentality behind the current monetary system, not as a claim about every white individual. Yes, China invented money around 5,000 years ago, and there’s debate about whether China or Sumerian got there first, but in its current form—this debt nonsense, this system where you can only rent, where you never truly own—that is a colonial mentality of money. It is a system that was exported, imposed, and now maintained globally. So, when I say, “white man’s thing,” I mean the system, not the skin. I look at farmers, for example, and I see people who voted for a system that makes sure the criminals exist. I’m not even talking about apartheid now. I’m talking about today’s modern democracy. They vote for the parties, the policies, the monetary system, the banking system. The government stays very quiet about that system. It denies people access to money and then sits back and watches them fight each other. This has been going on for many, many centuries. So, I don’t hate white people. I hate the system. I do hate those who still support the system—I’ll admit that a little bit—not because they’re white, but because they refuse to see what they’re defending. People don’t recognize the cruelty because most of them have a colonialist mentality. They don’t see it as cruel. It’s normal to them. They don’t understand where this cruelty eventually leads: to murders, to crime, to whole societies eating themselves alive.

In South Africa, 30 years ago, having a conversation with your parents about the monetary system was taboo. It was off limits. It made them very, very angry—to the point where, if you pushed the discussion any further, there was going to be violence. But now it’s fully visible. Now you can see why that was. They were not educated to think in that way. They were educated to not talk about it, because it served the interests of those who preferred people didn’t ask questions about this absurdity they call interest, criteria, responsible banking, moral hazard. They dress it up in respectable language, but it’s still a system that denies people access to money and then blames them for being poor. It creates criminals and then hates them. It creates slums and then hides them. It creates mountains of trash and then ships it to Nigeria or somewhere else so the West can pretend it doesn’t have a problem. So let me be clear: I am not race-hating. I am system-hating. I am not saying white people are the problem. I am saying the colonial mentality of money—the debt system, the banking system, the rentier system—is the problem. And anyone, of any race, who defends it is part of the problem. That includes farmers who voted for it, parents who refused to discuss it, economists who teach it, and governments who enforce it. They love to weaponize their favorite. Social weapons to shut down conversations, inflation and hyperinflation If you say somebody needs purchasing power, I pay inflation, inflation, currency debasement. But all that nonsense is happening anyway. They don’t want to hear about productive capacity. They just want the noise to stop. But the noise is the truth. And the truth is that the system is cruel. It always has been. Until people see that, nothing changes. The gold leaves. The trash stays. And the children pay for it.
